VIDEO.title: Jesus’ Final Warning Before Judgment… Are We Overlooking It?
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Matthew 24:36-51 · Episode 47 (#50 of 58 in the playlist)
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 24:36-51. No one knows that day and hour, not even the angels or the Son, but the Father alone. As in the days of Noah, people ate, drank and married until the flood took them all away; so will the coming of the Son of Man be. Two in the field, two women at the mill: one taken, one left. Stay awake, like a head of the house who knows a thief is coming. Who then is the faithful and prudent slave, found feeding the household when the master comes? The evil slave who says, 'My master is not coming for a long time,' is cut in pieces and put with the hypocrites.

'That day and hour' is the language of the day of Yahweh (Isaiah 13:6, 9; Ezekiel 13:5; Joel 1:15; Zephaniah 1:7). The video still reads the discourse as answering the disciples' question about the fall of the temple and Jerusalem, now filled with that imagery.

Noah's long work on the ark was itself a sign; when the flood came, it was sudden and severe. So with Jerusalem: about 40 years from the prophecy, and four years from the revolt of AD 66, with Galilee and other towns taken first. Eusebius reports that the Jerusalem church left for Pella before the war.

In Genesis 6, the earth was 'corrupt' (shachat) and God would 'destroy' (shachat) it: mankind had corrupted itself, so God destroyed it. Jesus sees the same in the corrupt leaders of His generation (23:34-36). God's household is the whole world, with the temple as a microcosm; the faithful slave keeps doing the master's work.

The lesson: in a world of corruption that the Lord will judge, God's people must focus more than ever on fulfilling their calling and the ultimate purpose for their creation. If they do this, they will be blessed on the day of God's judgment.
QUOTES: In a world of corruption that the Lord will judge, God's people must focus more than ever on fulfilling their calling and the ultimate purpose for their creation.
Every day that Noah built this gigantic structure was a sign to the people around him that God's judgment was coming.
Mankind had become so shachat that God shachat mankind.
The actual command of Jesus is not to spend countless hours determining the signs of his coming and when specifically that will be.

method.p: Look up a key word in the original language and trace where else it is used: in Genesis 6 one Hebrew verb means both 'corrupt' and 'destroy.'

src.text: “But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father alone.

lines.text: 'That day and hour' looks back to the disciples' question in 24:3 and imports the Old Testament day of Yahweh, applied here to the fall of the temple and Jerusalem.
The central concern is vigilance: Jesus does not want them caught off guard.
The video says Josephus tells of Vespasian attacking Jewish outposts at odd hours of the night to catch them by surprise (Jewish War, book 4).

left.text: For as in those days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noah entered the ark, and they did not understand until the flood came and took them all away; so will the coming of the Son of Man be.

right.text: they were eating, they were drinking, they were marrying, they were being given in marriage, until the day that Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all.

lines.text: The ark took a long time to build. Every day of building was a sign that judgment was coming; when the flood came, it was sudden and severe.
So with Jerusalem: around 40 years from prophecy to destruction, and four years from the revolt of AD 66, with Galilee and other towns taken first. Many trusted the walls and ignored the signs.

src.text: Then there will be two in the field; one will be taken, and one will be left. Two women will be grinding grain at the mill; one will be taken and one will be left. “Therefore stay awake, for you do not know which day your Lord is coming.

lines.text: In the video's reading, the ones taken are spared because they obeyed Jesus and remembered what He told them; the others are left to endure the judgment on the city.

Eusebius: 'the people of the church in Jerusalem had been commanded by a revelation, vouchsafed to approved men there before the war, to leave the city and to dwell in a certain town of Perea called Pella' (Church History 3.5.3).
Paul uses the thief image too: 'the day of the Lord will come just like a thief in the night' (1 Thessalonians 5:2).

src.text: Blow a trumpet in Zion, / And make a loud shout on My holy mountain! / Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, / For the day of Yahweh is coming; / Surely it is near, A day of darkness and thick darkness, / A day of clouds and dense gloom. / As the dawn is spread over the mountains, / So there is a numerous and mighty people; / There has never been anything like it, / Nor will there be again after it / For the years from generation to generation.

lines.text: The day of Yahweh comes with an army marching on a city, and 'The sun and the moon grow dark' (Joel 2:10), the way Jesus speaks in Matthew 24.

lines.text: Peter says Joel's promise is here at Pentecost, wonders and signs included (Acts 2:19-20). The culmination, in the video's reading, is the destruction of the temple and Jerusalem in AD 70.

left.text: And God saw the earth, and behold, it was corrupt; for all flesh had corrupted their way upon the earth.

right.text: Then God said to Noah, “The end of all flesh has come before Me; for the earth is filled with violence because of them; and behold, I am about to destroy them with the earth.

lines.text: The Hebrew shachat is used three times in 6:11-12 for 'corrupt,' then for God's 'destroy' in 6:13 and 6:17. Mankind corrupted itself, so God destroyed it.
The same pattern lies behind 'all these things will come upon this generation' (23:36).

src.text: “Who then is the faithful and prudent slave whom his master put in charge of his household to give them their food at the proper time? Blessed is that slave whom his master finds so doing when he comes. Truly I say to you that he will put him in charge of all his possessions.

lines.text: The master blesses the slave doing what he was told, feeding the household, not the one trying to work out when the master returns.
The disciples did not need to decode the signs: they would be obvious, and there would be time between the birth pains and the end to act as faithful servants.

left.text: God blessed them, and God said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth, and subdue it; and have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the sky and over every living thing that creeps on the earth.”

right.text: and you shall be to Me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.’ These are the words that you shall speak to the sons of Israel.”

lines.text: Dominion is borrowed authority: the world is God's house, and the temple, decorated with earthly and cosmic images, was its microcosm.
Humanity refused its mandate and became corrupt; so did the leaders of Jesus' day. Those who truly know God will replace them as a better kingdom of priests.

left.text: But if that evil slave says in his heart, ‘My master is not coming for a long time,’ and begins to beat his fellow slaves and eat and drink with drunkards; the master of that slave will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour which he does not know,

right.text: in whose case the god of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelieving so that they might not see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.

lines.text: The world is still corrupt; leaders in church and society still lead the flock astray. We keep spreading God's kingdom and shining the light of Christ until Jesus returns, whenever that is.
'Weeping and gnashing of teeth' (24:51) recurs in 8:12, 13:42, 13:50, 22:13 and 25:30.

The master's house and its people; in the video, God's world, with the temple as its microcosm.

BACKGROUND.p: Eusebius, writing in the early 300s, says the Jerusalem church was warned by a revelation before the war and moved to Pella. Many readers connect it with 'those who are in Judea must flee to the mountains' (24:16); some historians question the report.
The revolt began in AD 66. Vespasian took Galilee in 67, including Jotapata, and much of Judea by 68. After he became emperor, his son Titus besieged Jerusalem in AD 70.
Women ground grain daily on hand mills, often in pairs at a rotary quern, so two women at the mill is an everyday scene.

WITNESSES.text: But the people of the church in Jerusalem had been commanded by a revelation, vouchsafed to approved men there before the war, to leave the city and to dwell in a certain town of Perea called Pella.
So for this cause He spoke also of the days of Noe, for this cause He said too, Two shall be on the bed, signifying this, that He should come upon them thus unexpectedly.

DEBATES.h: Taken to safety, or taken away?
DEBATES.p: The video reads 'taken' as spared, like the Christians who fled. Others note that the flood 'took them all away' (24:39), so the one taken is swept away in judgment and the one left is spared.
The video applies 24:36-51 to the fall of Jerusalem. Many interpreters see a turn at 24:36 from the near event to the final coming, whose day no one knows.

DEBATES.h: The temple as a small cosmos
DEBATES.p: Some scholars argue that the temple was seen as a model of the world; others think the evidence for this is thinner in the first century.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: Pentecost came 50 days after Passover, about ten days after the ascension (Acts 1:3 gives forty days of appearances); the video says 50 days after Jesus ascended.
Eusebius credits the flight to Pella to 'a revelation, vouchsafed to approved men there before the war'; he does not say they remembered the Olivet Discourse.
The video counts eight woes in Matthew 23; the previous episode counted seven (eight with the bracketed 23:14).
The claim that Noah took 100 years to build the ark comes from later tradition; Genesis gives his age at 500 (5:32) and at the flood (7:6) but not the building time.
The Josephus account of night attacks is summarized from the video; it is not checked here.

QUESTIONS: Why does Jesus refuse to give a date?
In what ways was Noah's ark a sign to his neighbors?
What does 'shachat' teach about what corruption does to people?
What has the master given you to do 'at the proper time'?
Where are you tempted to say, 'My master is not coming for a long time'?
How can you keep doing the work of the kingdom in a corrupt world without fear?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson: in a world of corruption that the Lord will judge, God's people must focus more than ever on fulfilling their calling and the ultimate purpose for their creation. If they do, they will be blessed on the day of God's judgment. The all-seeing God wants to find His people busy with the work He has given them, out of the overflow of their relationship with Him. The world is still corrupt and the god of this age still blinds minds, so we keep spreading God's kingdom, trust the Lord, and put one foot in front of the other.

## Summary (from the video)
- The teacher reads Matthew 24:36-51. No one knows that day and hour, not even the angels or the Son, but the Father alone. As in the days of Noah, people ate, drank and married until the flood took them all away; so will the coming of the Son of Man be. Two in the field, two women at the mill: one taken, one left. Stay awake, like a head of the house who knows a thief is coming. Who then is the faithful and prudent slave, found feeding the household when the master comes? The evil slave who says, 'My master is not coming for a long time,' is cut in pieces and put with the hypocrites.
- 'That day and hour' is the language of the day of Yahweh (Isaiah 13:6, 9; Ezekiel 13:5; Joel 1:15; Zephaniah 1:7). The video still reads the discourse as answering the disciples' question about the fall of the temple and Jerusalem, now filled with that imagery.
- Noah's long work on the ark was itself a sign; when the flood came, it was sudden and severe. So with Jerusalem: about 40 years from the prophecy, and four years from the revolt of AD 66, with Galilee and other towns taken first. Eusebius reports that the Jerusalem church left for Pella before the war.
- In Genesis 6, the earth was 'corrupt' (shachat) and God would 'destroy' (shachat) it: mankind had corrupted itself, so God destroyed it. Jesus sees the same in the corrupt leaders of His generation (23:34-36). God's household is the whole world, with the temple as a microcosm; the faithful slave keeps doing the master's work.
- The lesson: in a world of corruption that the Lord will judge, God's people must focus more than ever on fulfilling their calling and the ultimate purpose for their creation. If they do this, they will be blessed on the day of God's judgment.

   (video) Humanity refused its mandate and became corrupt; so did the leaders of Jesus' day. Those who truly know God will replace them as a better kingdom of priests.
3. Matthew 24:48-51; 2 Corinthians 4:4: 'My master is not coming'
   Jesus (Matthew 24:48-50, LSB): "But if that evil slave says in his heart, ‘My master is not coming for a long time,’ and begins to beat his fellow slaves and eat and drink with drunkards; the master of that slave will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour which he does not know,"
   Paul (2 Corinthians 4:4, LSB): "in whose case the god of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelieving so that they might not see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God."
   (video) The world is still corrupt; leaders in church and society still lead the flock astray. We keep spreading God's kingdom and shining the light of Christ until Jesus returns, whenever that is.
   [Background] 'Weeping and gnashing of teeth' (24:51) recurs in 8:12, 13:42, 13:50, 22:13 and 25:30. (Matthew 8:12; Matthew 25:30)

## Key people
- Noah: His long work on the ark was a sign of coming judgment. [Background] Hebrews 11:7 and 2 Peter 2:5 call him a preacher of righteousness by faith.
- The faithful and prudent slave: Found feeding the household when the master comes. [Background] Luke 12:42-46 tells the same parable.
- The evil slave: Thinks he has all the time in the world. [Background] His end is with the hypocrites, as in chapter 23.
- Vespasian: Roman general who began the war. [Background] He subdued Galilee in AD 67, then became emperor in AD 69 and left the siege to his son Titus.
- Eusebius: Church historian who tells of the Christians' flight to Pella. [Background] Bishop of Caesarea; wrote his Church History in the early 300s.

## Places [Background]
- Jerusalem (named in the video): The city whose fall the disciples asked about (24:3).
- Pella (named in the video): Where Eusebius says the Jerusalem church went before the war.
- Jotapata: Galilean town Vespasian besieged in AD 67, where Josephus surrendered.
- Caesarea Maritima: Vespasian's headquarters for the war.

## Key terms
- Day of the Lord: The day of Yahweh: His coming in judgment, and salvation for His people (Joel 2; Zephaniah 1).
- Shachat: Hebrew verb meaning to corrupt or ruin, and to destroy (Genesis 6:11-17).
- Household: The master's house and its people; in the video, God's world, with the temple as its microcosm.
- Kingdom of priests: Israel's calling in Exodus 19:6, taken up for the church in 1 Peter 2:9.
- Pella: A city of the Decapolis east of the Jordan, where Eusebius says Jerusalem's Christians fled.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- The flight to Pella: Eusebius, writing in the early 300s, says the Jerusalem church was warned by a revelation before the war and moved to Pella. Many readers connect it with 'those who are in Judea must flee to the mountains' (24:16); some historians question the report.
- The Jewish War, AD 66-70: The revolt began in AD 66. Vespasian took Galilee in 67, including Jotapata, and much of Judea by 68. After he became emperor, his son Titus besieged Jerusalem in AD 70.
- Grinding at the mill: Women ground grain daily on hand mills, often in pairs at a rotary quern, so two women at the mill is an everyday scene.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- Eusebius of Caesarea (c. AD 325): "But the people of the church in Jerusalem had been commanded by a revelation, vouchsafed to approved men there before the war, to leave the city and to dwell in a certain town of Perea called Pella." Church History 3.5.3. NPNF 2.1 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "So for this cause He spoke also of the days of Noe, for this cause He said too, Two shall be on the bed, signifying this, that He should come upon them thus unexpectedly." Homilies on Matthew 77, on 24:40-41. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Watch therefore, for you know not what hour your Lord does come." Homilies on Matthew 77, quoting 24:42. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Taken to safety, or taken away? The video reads 'taken' as spared, like the Christians who fled. Others note that the flood 'took them all away' (24:39), so the one taken is swept away in judgment and the one left is spared.
- AD 70 or the final coming? The video applies 24:36-51 to the fall of Jerusalem. Many interpreters see a turn at 24:36 from the near event to the final coming, whose day no one knows.
- The temple as a small cosmos Some scholars argue that the temple was seen as a model of the world; others think the evidence for this is thinner in the first century.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- Pentecost came 50 days after Passover, about ten days after the ascension (Acts 1:3 gives forty days of appearances); the video says 50 days after Jesus ascended.
- Eusebius credits the flight to Pella to 'a revelation, vouchsafed to approved men there before the war'; he does not say they remembered the Olivet Discourse.
- The video counts eight woes in Matthew 23; the previous episode counted seven (eight with the bracketed 23:14).
- The claim that Noah took 100 years to build the ark comes from later tradition; Genesis gives his age at 500 (5:32) and at the flood (7:6) but not the building time.
- The Josephus account of night attacks is summarized from the video; it is not checked here.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why does Jesus refuse to give a date?
2. In what ways was Noah's ark a sign to his neighbors?
3. What does 'shachat' teach about what corruption does to people?
4. What has the master given you to do 'at the proper time'?
5. Where are you tempted to say, 'My master is not coming for a long time'?
6. How can you keep doing the work of the kingdom in a corrupt world without fear?

## Application
- (video) The lesson: in a world of corruption that the Lord will judge, God's people must focus more than ever on fulfilling their calling and the ultimate purpose for their creation. If they do, they will be blessed on the day of God's judgment. The all-seeing God wants to find His people busy with the work He has given them, out of the overflow of their relationship with Him. The world is still corrupt and the god of this age still blinds minds, so we keep spreading God's kingdom, trust the Lord, and put one foot in front of the other.
- Study note (added): write down the 'household' the Lord has put you over (family, work, church) and one way to 'give them their food at the proper time' this week.
